original.text:
athety ayam adhikārārthaḥ /
yogānuśāsanaṃ śāstram adhikṛtaṃ veditavyam /
yogaḥ samādhiḥ /
sa ca sārvabhaumaś cittasya dharmaḥ /
kṣiptaṃ mūḍhaṃ vikṣiptam ekāgraṃ niruddham iti cittabhūmayaḥ /
tatra vikṣipte cetasi vikṣepopasarjanībhūtaḥ samādhir na yogapakṣe vartate /
yas tv ekāgre cetasi sadbhūtam arthaṃ pradyotayati kṣiṇoti ca kleśān karmabandhanāni ślathayati nirodham abhimukhaṃ karoti sa saṃprajñāto yoga ity ākhyāyate /
sa ca vitarkānugato vicārānugata ānandānugato 'smitānugata ity upariṣṭān nivedayiṣyāmaḥ /
sarvavṛttinirodhe tv asaṃprajñātaḥ samādhiḥ
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: 'Now' (atha) marks that a topic is taken up (adhikāra): the treatise called 'the teaching of yoga' is to be understood as the subject in hand. Yoga is samādhi, and samādhi is a property of the mind (citta) at every level (sārvabhauma). The levels of the mind (citta-bhūmi) are: scattered (kṣipta), stupefied (mūḍha), distracted (vikṣipta), one-pointed (ekāgra) and stilled (niruddha). In a distracted mind, samādhi that has become subordinate to the distraction does not count on the side of yoga. But in the one-pointed mind, the samādhi that illumines the real object (sadbhūta artha), wears away the afflictions (kleśa), loosens the bonds of karma and turns the mind toward stilling (nirodha) is called samprajñāta yoga. That samādhi is accompanied by reasoning (vitarka), by reflection (vicāra), by joy (ānanda) or by I-am-ness (asmitā) — Vyāsa says he will set this out later. In the stilling of all activities, samādhi is asamprajñāta.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: J read this entry against the Sanskrit (full-check (random sample below 95%)); see ../fidelity.jsonl.

notes: Vyāsa here defines yoga as samādhi (not as the sūtra's own wording of 1.2) and lists the five levels of the mind; only the last two are said to belong to yoga in the full sense (the distracted level's samādhi is 'subordinate to distraction'). The closing words of the segment are the lead-in to 1.2 ('to state its mark this sūtra was begun').

original.text:
sā ca saṃprabodhe pratyavamarśāt pratyayaviśeṣaḥ /
katham, sukham aham asvāpsam /
prasannaṃ me manaḥ /
prajñāṃ me viśāradīkaroti /
duḥkham aham asvāpsam /
styānaṃ me mano bhramaty anavasthitam gāḍhaṃ mūḍho 'ham asvāpsam /
gurūṇi me gātrāṇi /
klāntaṃ me cittam /
alasaṃ muṣitam iva tiṣṭhatīti /
sa khalv ayaṃ prabuddhasya pratyavamarśo na syād asati pratyayānubhave tadāśritāḥ smṛtayś ca tadviṣayā na syuḥ /
tasmāt pratyayaviśeṣo nidrā /
sā ca samādhāv itarapratyayavan niroddhavyeti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: Sleep is a particular kind of cognition (pratyaya-viśeṣa), because on waking it is recollected (pratyavamarśa). How? One says: 'I slept happily; my mind is clear; it makes my understanding lucid.' Or: 'I slept in pain (duḥkham); my mind, dull (styāna), wanders unsteady.' Or: 'I slept deeply, stupefied (mūḍha); my limbs are heavy; my mind is weary; it stays sluggish, as if robbed.' This recollection by one awake would not occur if there were no experience of a cognition, and the memories resting on it and having it as object would not occur either. So sleep is a particular cognition. And like the other cognitions, it is to be stilled in samādhi.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

original.text:
kiṃ pratyayasya cittaṃ smaraty āhosvid viṣayasyeti /
grāhyoparaktaḥ pratyayo grāhyagrahaṇobhayākāranirbhāsas tajjātīyakaṃ saṃskāram ārabhate /
sa saṃskāraḥ svavyañjakāñjanas tadākārām eva grāhyagrahaṇobhayātmikāṃ smṛtiṃ janayati /
tatra grahaṇākārapūrvā buddhiḥ /
grāhyākārapūrvā smṛtiḥ /
sā ca dvayī --- bhāvitasmartavyā cābhāvitasmartavyā ca /
svapne bhāvitasmartavyā /
jāgratsamaye tv abhāvitasmartavyeti /
sarvāḥ smṛtayaḥ pramāṇaviparyayavikalpanidrāsmṛtīnām anubhavāt prabhavanti /
sarvāś caitā vṛttayaḥ sukhaduḥkhamohātmikāḥ /
sukhaduḥkhamohāś ca kleśeṣu vyākhyeyāḥ /
sukhānuśayī rāgaḥ /
duḥkhānuśayī dveṣaḥ /
mohaḥ punar avidyeti /
etāḥ sarvā vṛttayo niroddhavyāḥ /
āsāṃ nirodhe saṃprajñāto vā samādhir bhavaty asaṃprajñāto veti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: Does the mind remember the cognition or the object? A cognition coloured by the grasped (grāhya) shines with the double form of grasped and grasping and starts an impression (saṃskāra) of its own kind. When that impression is made manifest by its own manifester it produces a memory of just that form, consisting of both grasped and grasping. In the original cognition, the understanding (buddhi) has the form of grasping first; in memory the form of the grasped comes first. Memory is twofold: of what was cultivated (bhāvita-smartavya) and of what was not cultivated (abhāvita-smartavya); in dream the first, in the waking time the second. All memories arise from the experience of valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep and memory. All these activities are of the nature of pleasure, pain and delusion (sukha-duḥkha-moha), which are to be explained under the afflictions (kleśa): attachment (rāga) follows on pleasure, aversion (dveṣa) follows on pain, and delusion (moha) is ignorance (avidyā). All these activities are to be stilled; when they are stilled, samādhi comes about, either samprajñāta or asamprajñāta.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: J read this entry against the Sanskrit (full-check (random sample below 95%)); see ../fidelity.jsonl.

notes: The distinction between memory of the cultivated and of the uncultivated (dream vs waking) is stated without further explanation and is paraphrased as given. The link 'every activity is pleasure, pain or delusion; rāga follows pleasure, dveṣa follows pain, moha is avidyā' is the text's own bridge from the five activities to the afflictions. The segment ends with the lead-in to 1.12 ('what is the means for their stilling?').

original.text:
cittanadī nāmobhayatovāhinī vahati kalyāṇāya vahati pāpāya ca /
yā tu kaivalyaprāgbhārā vivekaviṣayanimnā sā kalyāṇavahā /
saṃsāraprāgbhārāvivekaviṣayaniṃnā pāpavahā /
tatra vairāgyeṇa viṣayasrotaḥ khilīkriyate /
vivekadarśanābhyāsena vivekasrota udghāṭyata ity ubhayādhīnaś cittavṛttinirodhaḥ
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: The river of the mind (citta-nadī) flows in both directions: it flows toward the good (kalyāṇa) and toward evil (pāpa). The one that inclines toward kaivalya, with its depth toward discernment (viveka), carries toward the good; the one that inclines toward saṃsāra, with its depth toward non-discernment, carries toward evil. Of these, by dispassion the stream toward objects is made barren (khilīkriyate); by the practice of the vision of discernment (viveka-darśana) the stream of discernment is opened. So the stilling of the mind's activities depends on both.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: J read this entry against the Sanskrit (full-check (random sample below 95%)); see ../fidelity.jsonl.

notes: The image of the mind as a river flowing both ways is Vyāsa's; the sūtra names only practice and dispassion.

original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)

paraphrase: Seen objects are, for example, women, food and drink, and lordship (aiśvarya). One is free of thirst for those; and free of thirst for heard-of objects — the attainment of heaven, of the bodiless state (vaidehya) and of merger in prakṛti (prakṛtilayatva). Even when divine or non-divine objects come into contact with him, the mind sees the fault in objects and, by the power of discerning insight (prasaṃkhyāna), has a consciousness of mastery that is without engagement (anābhoga-ātmikā) and empty of rejecting and taking (heya-upādeya-śūnyā). That is dispassion (vairāgya).
speaker: Vyāsa

original.text:
dṛṣṭānuśravikaviṣayadoṣadarśī viraktaḥ puruṣadarśanābhyāsāt tacchuddhipravivekāpyāyitabuddhir guṇebhyo vyaktāvyaktadharmakebhyo virakta iti /
tad dvayaṃ vairāgyam /
tatra yad uttaraṃ taj jñānaprasādamātram /
yasyodaye sati yogī pratyuditakhyātir evaṃ manyate --- prāptaṃ prāpaṇīyaṃ, kṣīṇāḥ kṣetavyāḥ kleśāḥ, chinnaḥ śliṣṭaparvā bhavasaṃkramaḥ, yasyāvicchedāj janitvā mriyate mṛtvā ca jāyata iti /
jñānasyaiva parā kāṣṭhā vairāgyam /
etasyaiva hi nāntarīyakaṃ kaivalyam
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: One who has seen the fault in seen and scripture-taught objects is dispassionate; by the practice of the vision of the puruṣa, his understanding (buddhi) is refreshed by the discernment of the puruṣa's purity, and he is dispassionate toward the guṇas, whose properties are manifest and unmanifest. So dispassion is twofold. Of the two, the latter is only the clearness (prasāda) of knowledge. When it arises, the yogin in whom discernment has risen thinks: 'What was to be attained is attained; the afflictions to be destroyed are destroyed; the linked chain of becoming (bhava-saṃkrama), by whose unbroken continuance one is born and dies and after dying is born again, is cut.' The highest limit (parā kāṣṭhā) of knowledge is dispassion; kaivalya is inseparably bound to it (nāntarīyaka).
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: J read this entry against the Sanskrit (full-check (random sample below 95%)); see ../fidelity.jsonl.

notes: Vyāsa says dispassion is 'twofold' (tad dvayaṃ vairāgyam) and calls the second 'only the clearness of knowledge'; the sūtra itself labels it 'para'. The yogin's thought ('what was to be attained is attained…') is Vyāsa's description of how this dispassion shows itself. The segment ends with the lead-in to 1.17.

original.text:
vitarkaś cittasyālambane sthūla ābhogaḥ /
sūkṣmo vicāraḥ /
ānando hlādaḥ /
ekātmikā saṃvid asmitā /
tatra prathamaś catuṣṭayānugataḥ samādhiḥ savitarkaḥ /
dvitīyo vitarkavikalaḥ savicāraḥ /
tṛtīyo vicāravikalaḥ sānandaḥ /
caturthas tadvikalo 'smitāmātra iti /
sarva ete sālambanāḥ samādhayaḥ
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: Reasoning (vitarka) is the mind's gross engagement (ābhoga) with its support (ālambana); reflection (vicāra) is the subtle one; joy (ānanda) is delight (hlāda); I-am-ness (asmitā) is awareness (saṃvid) whose nature is single-selved (ekātmikā). Of these, the first samādhi, accompanied by all four, is 'with reasoning' (savitarka); the second, lacking reasoning, is 'with reflection' (savicāra); the third, lacking reflection, is 'with joy' (sānanda); the fourth, lacking that too, is 'I-am-ness alone' (asmitāmātra). All these samādhis are with a support (sālambana).
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: J read this entry against the Sanskrit (full-check (random sample below 95%)); see ../fidelity.jsonl.

notes: Vyāsa gives the four as successive subtractions: each later samādhi lacks the previous accompaniment. The segment ends with the lead-in to 1.18 ('what is the means and the nature of asamprajñāta samādhi?').

original.text:
sarvavṛttipratyastamaye saṃskāraśeṣo nirodhaś cittasya samādhir asaṃprajñātaḥ /
tasya paraṃ vairāgyam upāyaḥ /
sālambano hy abhyāsas tatsādhanāya na kalpata iti virāmapratyayo nirvastuka ālambanīkriyate /
sa cārthaśūnyaḥ /
tadabhyāsapūrvakaṃ hi cittaṃ nirālambanam abhāvaprāptam iva bhavatīty eṣa nirbījaḥ samādhir asaṃprajñātaḥ
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: When all activities have set (pratyastamaya), the stilling of the mind with only impressions remaining (saṃskāra-śeṣa) is samādhi called asamprajñāta. Its means is the higher dispassion (para vairāgya). Practice that rests on a support (sālambana) is not fit to bring this about; so the cognition of cessation (virāma-pratyaya), which has no real thing behind it (nirvastuka) and is empty of an object, is taken as the support. The mind that has practised that becomes without support (nirālambana), as if it had reached non-being; this is seedless (nirbīja) samādhi, asamprajñāta. The bhāṣya then says it is of two kinds, from means (upāya-pratyaya) and from birth (bhava-pratyaya), and that the first belongs to yogins.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: J read this entry against the Sanskrit (random-10pct, full-check (random sample below 95%)); see ../fidelity.jsonl.

notes: Vyāsa's phrase 'as if it had reached non-being' (abhāvaprāptam iva) is 'as if'; the text does not say the mind ceases to exist. The 'cognition of cessation' as a support that is itself empty of an object is compressed in the Sanskrit; the paraphrase keeps the minimal sense.

videhānāṃ devānāṃ bhavapratyayaḥ /
te hi svasaṃskāramātropayogena cittena kaivalyapadam ivānubhavantaḥ svasaṃskāravipākaṃ tathājātīyakam ativāhayanti /
tathā prakṛtilayāḥ sādhikāre cetasi prakṛtilīne kaivalyapadam ivānubhavanti, yāvan na punar āvartate 'dhikāravaśāc cittam iti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)

Likewise those merged in prakṛti (prakṛti-laya), whose mind, still holding an office (sādhikāra), is merged in prakṛti, experience as it were the state of kaivalya, until the mind returns again through the force of that office.

sarvaśabdāgrahaṇāt saṃprajñāto 'pi yoga ity ākhyāyate /
cittaṃ hi prakhyāpravṛttisthitiśīlatvāt triguṇam /
prakhyārūpaṃ hi cittasattvaṃ rajastamobhyāṃ saṃsṛṣṭam aiśvaryaviṣayapriyaṃ bhavati /

citiśaktir apariṇāminy apratisaṃkramā darśitaviṣayā śuddhā cānantā ca sattvaguṇātmikā ceyam ato viparītā vivekakhyātir iti /
atas tasyāṃ viraktaṃ cittaṃ tām api khyātiṃ niruṇaddhi /
tadavasthaṃ saṃskāropagaṃ bhavati /
sa nirbījaḥ samādhiḥ /
na tatra kiṃcit saṃprajñāyata ity asaṃprajñātaḥ /
dvividhaḥ sa yogaś cittavṛttinirodha iti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: Because the word 'all' (sarva) is not taken in the sūtra, samprajñāta too is called yoga. The mind (citta) has three guṇas, because its nature is illumination (prakhyā), activity (pravṛtti) and steadiness/inertia (sthiti). Its sattva, whose form is illumination, when mixed with rajas and tamas becomes fond of lordship (aiśvarya) and sense-objects. The same, pierced by tamas, goes toward what is not dharma (adharma), ignorance (ajñāna), non-dispassion (avairāgya) and non-lordship (anaiśvarya). The same, when the covering of delusion has been worn away, shining in every direction and touched only by a measure of rajas, goes toward dharma, knowledge (jñāna), dispassion (vairāgya) and lordship. The same, freed from even a trace of the taint of rajas, established in its own form, reduced to the discernment of the difference between sattva and puruṣa, goes to the meditation of the cloud of dharma (dharmamegha-dhyāna); meditators call this the supreme discerning insight (prasaṃkhyāna). The power of consciousness (citi-śakti) is unchanging (apariṇāminī), does not pass over into anything (apratisaṃkramā), shows the objects (darśita-viṣayā), is pure and unending; but this discernment (vivekakhyāti) is of the nature of the sattva-guṇa and so is the opposite of it. The mind, dispassionate even toward that, stills that discernment too; in that state it holds only impressions (saṃskāra) — that is seedless samādhi (nirbīja). Nothing is fully known there, hence it is asamprajñāta. Thus yoga, the stilling of the mind's activities, is twofold.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: Samādhi from means (upāya-pratyaya) belongs to yogins. Faith (śraddhā) is serenity (saṃprasāda) of the mind; like a kind mother it protects the yogin. In one who has faith and seeks discernment (viveka), energy (vīrya) arises; in one in whom energy has arisen, mindfulness (smṛti) stands present; when mindfulness is present the mind, unagitated, is concentrated (samādhīyate); in one whose mind is concentrated, the discernment of insight (prajñā-viveka) comes about, by which he knows the thing as it is. From the practice of that, and from dispassion toward each of its objects, asamprajñāta samādhi comes about. The bhāṣya then says these yogins are of nine kinds by their means (mild, middling, intense) and, within each, by ardor (saṃvega: mild, middling, intense).
speaker: Vyāsa

kuśalākuśalāni karmāṇi /

yathā muktasya pūrvā bandhakoṭiḥ prajñāyate naivam īśvarasya /
yathā vā prakṛtilīnasyottarā bandhakoṭiḥ saṃbhāvyate naivam īśvarasya /
sa tu sadaiva muktaḥ sadaiveśvara iti /
yo 'sau prakṛṣṭasattvopādānād īśvarasya śāśvatika utkarṣaḥ sa kiṃ sanimitta āhosvin nirnimitta iti /

etasmād etad bhavati sadaiveśvaraḥ sadaiva mukta iti /
tac ca tasyaiśvaryaṃ sāmyātiśayavinirmuktam /
na tāvad aiśvaryāntareṇa tad atiśayyate /
yad evātiśayi syāt tad eva tat syāt /
tasmād yatra kāṣṭhāprāptir aiśvaryasya sa īśvara iti /
na ca tatsamānam aiśvaryam asti /
kasmāt, dvayos tulyayor ekasmin yugapatkāmite 'rthe navam idam astu purāṇam idam astv ity ekasya siddhāv itarasya prākāmyavighātād ūnatvaṃ prasaktam /

paraphrase: The afflictions (kleśa) are ignorance and the rest; actions (karma) are skilful and unskilful; ripening (vipāka) is their fruit; the residues (āśaya) are the tendencies (vāsanā) suited to them. These abide in the mind but are attributed to the puruṣa, since he is the enjoyer of their fruit, as victory or defeat abiding in the warriors is attributed to the master. The one untouched by this enjoyment is the special puruṣa, Īśvara. Objection: there are many liberated ones (kevalin) who have cut three bonds. But Īśvara's connection with those bonds (tat-saṃbandha) neither has been nor will be. The liberated one's earlier limit of bondage is known; not so Īśvara's. The one merged in prakṛti may have a later limit of bondage; not so Īśvara. He is ever free, ever Īśvara. His eternal excellence rests on the taking up of supreme sattva; its cause is scripture (śāstra), and scripture's cause is supreme sattva; the connection of these two is beginningless. His lordship is free from equal and greater: two equals cannot each have an object wished at once (e.g. 'let this be new' and 'let this be old'), since the objects conflict, so one's success would obstruct the other's free will. Whoever's lordship is free from equal and surpassing is Īśvara, and he is a special puruṣa.

paraphrase: This supersensible grasp (atīndriya-grahaṇa) of past, future and present things, singly and together, small or great, is the seed of omniscience; where, growing, it is unsurpassed, that one is omniscient. Since the seed of omniscience shows degrees, like measure it must reach a limit; where knowledge reaches its limit is the omniscient one, and he is a special puruṣa. Inference, once it has concluded only the general, is spent and cannot establish a particular; his name and particular features are to be sought from scripture (āgama). He has no benefit for himself, but his purpose is the benefit of beings: 'by teaching knowledge and dharma I will raise saṃsāra-bound puruṣas in the dissolutions of the aeon and the great dissolution.' And it is said: the first knower (ādividvān), the blessed supreme seer, taking up a created mind (nirmāṇa-citta) out of compassion, taught the tantra to Āsuri who wished to know.

paraphrase: The nine obstacles are distractions (vikṣepa) of the mind. They occur together with the mind's activities (citta-vṛtti); when they are absent, the activities spoken of before do not occur. Illness (vyādhi) is disorder (vaiṣamya) of the bodily constituents (dhātu), the humours (rasa) and the organs (karaṇa). Dullness (styāna) is unfitness of the mind for work (akarmaṇyatā). Doubt (saṃśaya) is cognition touching both alternatives: 'this may be so, it may not be so'. Heedlessness (pramāda) is not cultivating the means of samādhi. Laziness (ālasya) is non-engagement (apravṛtti) due to heaviness (gurutva) of the body and of the mind. Non-abstention (avirati) is greed (gardha) of the mind, which consists in contact with sense-objects. Erroneous vision (bhrānti-darśana) is knowledge that is error (viparyaya). Failure to gain a stage (alabdha-bhūmikatva) is non-attainment of a ground (bhūmi) of samādhi. Instability (anavasthitatva) is the mind's not being established on a ground that has been gained; for when samādhi has been attained it would remain established. These distractions of the mind are called the nine taints of yoga (yoga-mala), enemies of yoga (yoga-pratipakṣa) and obstacles to yoga (yogāntarāya).
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: To remove distraction, one should practise with the mind resting on a single principle (eka-tattva). The bhāṣya then argues against the view that the mind is only a cognition fixed to one object each and momentary (pratyartha-niyata, kṣaṇika): for such a view every mind would be one-pointed and none distracted. If cognitions were different by nature and unconnected by one mind, how could one remember what another saw, or one be the enjoyer of karma-store built by another? The cognition 'I' (aham) — 'what I saw I now touch; what I touched I now see' — stands as one across the different cognitions, is grasped by one's own experience, and the power of perception is not overcome by another means of knowing. Hence the mind is one and has many objects, and it persists.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: J read this entry against the Sanskrit (full-check (random sample below 95%)); see ../fidelity.jsonl.

notes: Vyāsa states the practice in one sentence and then argues at length against a view he does not name (that the mind is momentary and limited to one object per cognition). The opposing view is recorded in the wording Vyāsa gives it; commentators name the opponent, but that is not in this passage. Vyāsa's own conclusion is that the mind is one, has many objects, and abides (ekam anekārtham avasthitaṃ cittam).

paraphrase: For one who holds [the mind] at the tip of the nose, the awareness of divine smell is 'the activity of smell' (gandha-pravṛtti); at the tip of the tongue, awareness of taste; at the palate, awareness of form (colour); in the middle of the tongue, awareness of touch; at the root of the tongue, awareness of sound. These activities, when they arise, bind the mind to steadiness, dispel doubt (saṃśaya), and become a doorway (dvāra) to the insight of samādhi. The same is to be understood of activities that arise about the moon, sun, planets, jewels, lamps and rays, which are also concerned with an object. What is learned from scripture, inference and a teacher's instruction is true, yet as long as even one part is not known by one's own experience, all remains as if beyond sight and does not give firm conviction about subtle matters such as liberation (apavarga). So, to reinforce scripture, inference and teacher, some particular thing must certainly be made directly perceived; when one part of what was taught is directly known, all the subtle matters, up to liberation, are trusted. This mind-preparation (citta-parikarma) is taught for this. With the consciousness of mastery (vaśīkāra-saṃjñā) arisen in the varied activities, the mind becomes able to make each thing directly perceived; and then faith, energy, mindfulness and samādhi will arise unobstructed.

cittam ayaskāntamaṇikalpaṃ saṃnidhimātropakāri dṛśyatvena svaṃ bhavati puruṣasya svāminaḥ /
tasmāc cittavṛttibodhe puruṣasyānādiḥ saṃbandho hetuḥ
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: In emergence (vyutthāna), the puruṣa has an activity not distinguished from whatever activities the mind has. So a sūtra [quoted] says: 'Seeing is one alone; discernment (khyāti) alone is seeing.' The mind is like a magnet (ayaskānta-maṇi): it helps merely by being near, and by being seen it becomes the possession of the puruṣa, its master. Therefore the beginningless connection of the puruṣa with the mind is the cause of the awareness of the mind's activities.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

original.text:
sūkṣme niviśamānasya paramāṇvantaṃ sthitipadaṃ labhata iti /
sthūle niviśamānasya paramamahattvāntaṃ sthitipadaṃ cittasya /
evaṃ tām ubhayīṃ koṭim anudhāvato yo 'syāpratīghātaḥ sa paro vaśīkāraḥ /
tadvaśīkārāt paripūrṇaṃ yoginaś cittaṃ na punar abhyāsakṛtaṃ parikarmāpekṣata iti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: For one entering the subtle, the mind's footing extends up to the atom; for one entering the gross, up to the greatest magnitude. The unobstructedness (apratīghāta) of one who runs to both limits is the supreme mastery (para vaśīkāra). By that mastery the yogin's mind is complete (paripūrṇa) and no longer needs further preparation (parikarma) made by practice. The closing lines lead to the next question: what is the nature and object of coalescence (samāpatti) for a mind that has gained steadiness.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

kṣīṇavṛtter iti pratyastamitapratyayasyety arthaḥ /
abhijātasyeva maṇer iti dṛṣṭāntopādānam /
yathā sphaṭika upāśrayabhedāt tattadrūpoparakta upāśrayarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate tathā grāhyālambanoparaktaṃ cittaṃ grāhyasamāpannaṃ grāhyasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate /
bhūtasūkṣmoparaktaṃ bhūtasūkṣmasamāpannaṃ bhūtasūkṣmasvarūpābhāsaṃ bhavati /
tathā sthūlālambanoparaktaṃ sthūlarūpasamāpannaṃ sthūlarūpābhāsaṃ bhavati /
tathā viśvabhedoparaktaṃ viśvabhedasamāpannaṃ viśvarūpābhāsaṃ bhavati /
tathā grahaṇeṣv apīndriyeṣv api draṣṭavyam /
grahaṇālambanoparaktaṃ grahaṇasamāpannaṃ grahaṇasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate /
tathā grahītṛpuruṣālambanoparaktaṃ grahītṛpuruṣasamāpannaṃ grahītṛpuruṣasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsate /
tathā muktapuruṣālambanoparaktaṃ muktapuruṣasamāpannaṃ muktapuruṣasvarūpākāreṇa nirbhāsata iti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: 'Of one whose activities have dwindled' means one whose cognitions have set (pratyastamita-pratyaya). 'Like a flawless crystal' is an example: as a crystal, according to what it rests on, shines with the form of that support, so the mind coloured by a graspable support appears in the form of that graspable thing. Coloured by the subtle elements, it appears as the form of the subtle elements; by a gross support, in gross form; by the varieties of the world, in the form of the world. The same is to be seen with the instruments of grasping (the sense faculties): coloured by them, it appears in their form. Likewise coloured by the puruṣa as knower it appears in his form; and coloured by the liberated puruṣa (mukta-puruṣa) it appears in the form of the liberated puruṣa. So the mind, like a flawless crystal, in respect of knower, instrument and known, has the taking on of the form of what it stands in; this is called coalescence (samāpatti).
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

original.text:
tadyathā gaur iti śabdo gaur ity artho gaur iti jñānam ity avibhāgena vibhaktānām api grahaṇaṃ dṛṣṭam /
vibhajyamānāś cānye śabdadharmā anye 'rthadharmā anye vijñānadharmā ity eteṣāṃ vibhaktaḥ panthāḥ /
tatra samāpannasya yogino yo gavādyarthaḥ samādhiprajñāyāṃ samārūḍhaḥ sa cec chabdārthajñānavikalpānuviddha upāvartate sā saṃkīrṇā samāpattiḥ savitarkety ucyate. 1.42
yadā punaḥ śabdasaṃketasmṛtipariśuddhau śrutānumānajñānavikalpaśūnyāyāṃ samādhiprajñāyāṃ svarūpamātreṇāvasthito 'rthas tatsvarūpākāramātratayaivāvacchidyate /
sā ca nirvitarkā samāpattiḥ /
tat paraṃ pratyakṣam /
tac ca śrutānumānayor bījam /
tataḥ śrutānumāne prabhavataḥ /
na ca śrutānumānajñānasahabhūtaṃ tad darśanam /
tasmād asaṃkīrṇaṃ praṃmāṇāntareṇa yogino nirvitarkasamādhijaṃ darśanam iti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: Example: 'cow' as word, 'cow' as object, 'cow' as cognition — though distinct, they are seen taken together without division; and when divided, the properties of the word are one thing, of the object another, of the cognition another: their paths are separate. When the object (a cow, etc.) has risen into the samādhi-insight (samādhi-prajñā) of a yogin in coalescence, if it stands mixed with the conceptual constructions of word, object and cognition, that is the mixed (saṃkīrṇa) coalescence called savitarkā. But when, on the purification of the memory of word-convention, the samādhi-insight is empty of the constructions of scriptural and inferential knowledge, and the object stands only in its own form, defined only by the form of that form, that is nirvitarkā coalescence. It is the supreme perception (pratyakṣa), and the seed of testimony and inference; from it testimony and inference arise; and that seeing does not go along with knowledge from testimony and inference. So the seeing born of nirvitarka samādhi in the yogin is unmixed (asaṃkīrṇa) with any other means of knowing.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

original.text:
yā śabdasaṃketaśrutānumānajñānavikalpasmṛtipariśuddhau grāhyasvarūpa.uparaktā prajñā svam iva prajñāsvarūpaṃ grahaṇātmakaṃ tyaktvā padārthamātrasvarūpā grāhyasvarūpāpanneva bhavati sā tadā nirvitarkā samāpattiḥ /
tathā ca vyākyātaṃ tasyā ekabuddhyupakramo hy arthātmāṇupracayaviśeṣātmā gavādir ghaṭādir vā lokaḥ /
sa ca saṃsthānaviśeṣo bhūtasūkṣmāṇāṃ sādhāraṇo dharma ātmabhūtaḥ phalena vyaktenānumitaḥ svavyañjakāñjanaḥ prādurbhavati /
dharmāntarasya kapālāder udaye ca tirobhavati /
sa eṣa dharmo 'vayavīty ucyate /
yo 'sāv ekaś ca mahāṃś cāṇīṃyaś ca sparśavāṃś ca kriyādharmakaś cānityaś ca tenāvayavinā vyavahārāḥ kriyante /
yasya punar avastukaḥ sa pracayaviśeṣaḥ /
sūkṣmaṃ ca kāraṇam anupalabhyam avikalpasya tasyāvayavyabhāvād atadrūpapratiṣṭhaṃ mithyājñānam iti prāyeṇa sarvam eva prāptaṃ mithyājñānam iti /
tadā ca samyagjñānam api kiṃ syād viṣayābhāvāt /
yad yad upalabhyate tat tad avayavitvenāmnātam /
tasmād asty avayavī yo mahattvādivyavahārāpannaḥ samāpatter nirvitarkāyā viṣayī bhavati
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: When the memory of word-convention, of scriptural and of inferential knowledge and of constructions is purified, the insight (prajñā) that was coloured by the form of the grasped, leaving aside as it were its own grasping form, becomes as if it had the form of the thing-meaning alone; it is then nirvitarkā coalescence. As was explained: its object is a whole (avayavin) — the 'world', a cow or a pot, of the form of a particular aggregation of atoms, grasped in one act of understanding; it appears as a shared property of the subtle elements, inferred from its manifest fruit, coloured by what manifests it, and disappears when another property (e.g. potsherds) arises. This property is called the whole. It is one, great or very small, touchable, active and impermanent; ordinary dealings are carried out with it. If the aggregation were a non-thing, then, the subtle cause not being perceived and there being no whole, almost everything would be false knowledge (mithyā-jñāna), 'established in a form not its own'; then even right knowledge would have no object. Whatever is perceived is taught as whole; so the whole exists, which has come to ordinary dealings about greatness and the like and is the object of nirvitarkā coalescence.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: J read this entry against the Sanskrit (low-confidence, full-check (random sample below 95%)); see ../fidelity.jsonl.

notes: Compressed and difficult (the Sanskrit contains a typographical '.uparaktā' in the edition; the original is copied exactly). Vyāsa here argues that the whole (avayavin) is real, against a view that the aggregation is not a real thing (avastuka); he does not name the opponent. Paraphrase keeps the minimal sense: nirvitarkā has the thing itself, not word or memory, as its content, and Vyāsa holds the whole to be real.

original.text:
tatra bhūtasūkṣmakeṣv abhivyaktadharmakeṣu deśakālanimittānubhavāvacchinneṣu yā samāpattiḥ sā savicārety ucyate /
tatrāpy ekabuddhinirgrāhyam evoditadharmaviśiṣṭaṃ bhūtasūkṣmam ālambanībhūtaṃ samādhiprajñāyām upatiṣṭhate /
yā punaḥ sarvathā sarvataḥ śāntoditāvyapadeśyadharmānavacchinneṣu sarvadharmānupātiṣu sarvadharmātmakeṣu samāpattiḥ sā nirvicārety ucyate /
evaṃsvarūpaṃ hi tadbhūtasūkṣmam etenaiva svarūpeṇālambanībhūtam eva samādhiprajñāsvarūpam uparañjayati /
prajñā ca svarūpaśūnyevārthamātrā yadā bhavati tadā nirvicārety ucyate /
tatra mahadvastuviṣayā savitarkā nirvitarkā ca, sūkṣmavastuviṣayā savicārā nirvicārā ca /
evam ubhayor etayaiva nirvitarkayā vikalpahānir vyākhyāteti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: Coalescence on the subtle elements (bhūta-sūkṣma) whose properties are manifest, limited by place, time and cause-experience, is called savicārā. Even there, the subtle element endowed with a risen property, graspable by one understanding, stands as support in the samādhi-insight. Coalescence on those [subtle elements] that are in every way and on every side not limited by quiescent, risen or unspecifiable properties (śānta-udita-avyapadeśya-dharma-anavacchinna), which follow all properties and have all properties as their nature, is called nirvicārā: the subtle element stands as support just in its own form, colouring the samādhi-insight; and when the insight is as if empty of its own form, with the object alone, it is called nirvicārā. Thus, savitarkā and nirvitarkā have a gross object; savicārā and nirvicārā a subtle object. In this way, the giving up of construction (vikalpa) in both is explained by the nirvitarkā.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

pārthivasyāṇor gandhatanmātraṃ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ /
āpyasya rasatanmātram /
taijasasya rūpatanmātram /
vāyavīyasya sparśatanmātram /
ākāśasya śabdatanmātram iti /
teṣām ahaṃkāraḥ /
asyāpi liṅgamātraṃ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ /
liṅgamātrasyāpy aliṅgaṃ sūkṣmo viṣayaḥ /
na cāliṅgāt paraṃ sūkṣmam asti /
nanv asti puruṣaḥ sūkṣma iti satyam /
yathā liṅgāt param aliṅgasya saukṣmyaṃ na caivaṃ puruṣasya /
kiṃtu, liṅgasyānvayikāraṇaṃ puruṣo na bhavati, hetus tu bhavatīti /
ataḥ pradhāne saukṣmyaṃ niratiśayaṃ vyākhyātam
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: The subtle object of an atom of earth is the smell-tanmātra; of water, the taste-tanmātra; of fire, the form-tanmātra; of air, the touch-tanmātra; of ether, the sound-tanmātra. Of these, the subtle object is the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); of that, the mere mark (liṅga-mātra); of the mere mark, the unmarked (aliṅga). There is nothing subtler beyond the unmarked. Objection: the puruṣa is subtle. Granted; but the puruṣa is not subtler than the marked in the way the unmarked is subtler than the mark: the puruṣa is not the material cause (anvayi-kāraṇa) of the mark, but only a cause (hetu). So the subtlety in the primal (pradhāna) is explained as unsurpassed.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

fidelity.note: J read this entry against the Sanskrit (full-check (random sample below 95%)); see ../fidelity.jsonl.

notes: Vyāsa's ladder of subtlety: the five tanmātras, ahaṃkāra, liṅga-mātra, aliṅga (pradhāna). He says the puruṣa is not to be counted on that ladder: it is a cause (hetu) but not the material cause of the mark.

original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)

aśuddhyāvaraṇamalāpetasya prakāśātmano buddhisattvasya rajastamobhyām anabhibhūtaḥ svacchaḥ sthitipravāho vaiśāradyam /
yadā nirvicārasya samādher vaiśāradyam idaṃ jāyate tadā yogino bhavaty adhyātmaprasādo bhūtārthaviṣayaḥ kramānanurodhī sphuṭaḥ prajñālokaḥ /

original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)

paraphrase: Lucidity (vaiśāradya) is the clear, steady flow (sthiti-pravāha) of the luminous buddhi-sattva, freed from the taint of impurity and covering, not overcome by rajas and tamas. When this lucidity of nirvicāra samādhi arises, the yogin has inner clarity (adhyātma-prasāda): the light of insight (prajñāloka), concerned with things as they are, not following sequence, distinct. And it is said: 'Having climbed the terrace of insight, the wise one, free from sorrow, looks on the sorrowing people, as one on a mountain looks on those standing on the ground.'
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

And it is said: 'By scripture, by inference, and by the relish of the practice of meditation — forming insight in these three ways one obtains the highest yoga.'

śrutam āgamavijñānaṃ tat sāmānyaviṣayam /
na hy āgamena śakyo viśeṣo 'bhidhātum, kasmāt, na hi viśeṣeṇa kṛtasaṃketaḥ śabda iti /
tathānumānaṃ sāmānyaviṣayam eva /
yatra prāptis tatra gatir yatrāprāptis tatra na bhavati gatir ity uktam /
anumānena ca sāmānyenopasaṃhāraḥ /
tasmāc chrutānumānaviṣayo na viśeṣaḥ kaścid astīti /
na cāsya sūkṣmavyavahitaviprakṛṣṭasya vastuno lokapratyakṣeṇa grahaṇam asti /
na cāsya viśeṣasyāpramāṇakasyābhāvo 'stīti samādhiprajñānirgrāhya eva sa viśeṣo bhavati bhūtasūkṣmagato vā puruṣagato vā /
tasmāc chrutānumānaprajñābhyām anyaviṣayā sā prajñā viśeṣārthatvād iti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)

paraphrase: Śruta is knowledge from scripture (āgama), and its object is the general (sāmānya): a particular cannot be stated by scripture, since a word has no convention laid down for a particular. Inference too has only the general as object: it is said that where there is arrival, there is going; and inference concludes in a general way. So no particular is the object of testimony and inference. This particular, subtle, hidden or far away, is not grasped by ordinary perception either; nor is its non-existence established, since there is no proof of that. So that particular is grasped only by the samādhi-insight, whether in the subtle elements or in the puruṣa. Hence this insight has an object other than that of testimony and inference, because its purport is a particular.
speaker: Vyāsa

kleśahetukāḥ karmāśayapracaye kṣetrībhūtāḥ kliṣṭāḥ /
khyātiviṣayā guṇādhikāravirodhinyo 'kliṣṭāḥ /
kliṣṭapravāhapatitā apy akliṣṭāḥ /
kliṣṭacchidreṣv apy akliṣṭā bhavanti /
akliṣṭacchideṣu kliṣṭā iti /
tathājātīyakāḥ saṃskārā vṛttibhir eva kriyante /
saṃskāraiś ca vṛttaya iti /
evaṃ vṛttisaṃskāracakram aniśam āvartate /
tad evaṃbhūtaṃ cittam avasitādhikāram ātmakalpena vyavatiṣṭhate pralayaṃ vā gacchatīti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: Afflicted (kliṣṭa) activities are those caused by the afflictions (kleśa), which become the field (kṣetra) in which the store of karma (karmāśaya) is heaped up. Unafflicted (akliṣṭa) activities have discernment (khyāti) as their object and oppose the dominion of the guṇas. Even unafflicted ones that occur within the stream of afflicted ones remain unafflicted; in the gaps of the afflicted, unafflicted ones arise, and in the gaps of the unafflicted, afflicted ones. Impressions (saṃskāra) of the same kind are produced by the activities, and activities by the impressions: so the wheel of activity and impression (vṛtti-saṃskāra-cakra) turns without ceasing. The mind so constituted, once its task is complete, either stays on as if it were the self (ātmakalpena) or goes to dissolution (pralaya). Thus the activities are fivefold, afflicted and unafflicted.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

original.text:
samādhiprajñāprabhavaḥ saṃskāro vyutthānasaṃskārāśayaṃ bādhate /
vyutthānasaṃskārābhibhavāt tatprabhavāḥ pratyayā na bhavanti /
pratyayanirodhe samādhir upatiṣṭhate /
tataḥ samādhijā prajñā, tataḥ prajñākṛtāḥ saṃskārā iti navo navaḥ saṃskārāśayo jāyate /
tataś ca prajñā, tataś ca saṃskārā iti /
katham asau saṃskārātiśayaś cittaṃ sādhikāraṃ na kariṣyatīti /
na te prajñākṛtāḥ saṃskārāḥ kleśakṣayahetutvāc cittam adhikāraviśiṣṭaṃ kurvanti /
cittaṃ hi te svakāryād avasādayanti /
khyātiparyavasānaṃ hi cittaceṣṭitam iti
original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)

paraphrase: The impression (saṃskāra) born of samādhi-insight obstructs the store of impressions of emergence (vyutthāna-saṃskāra-āśaya). With the overcoming of the impressions of emergence, the cognitions born of them do not arise. With the stilling of cognitions, samādhi is present; from it, insight (prajñā); from that, impressions made by insight: so a new store of impressions arises again and again, and from it insight, and from that impressions. How will this excess of impressions not give the mind an office (adhikāra) again? Those impressions made by insight do not give the mind a further office, because they cause the wearing away of the afflictions (kleśa-kṣaya); for they make the mind sink from its own work, since the mind's whole striving ends in discernment (khyāti-paryavasāna).
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

sa na kevalaṃ samādhiprajñāvirodhī prajñākṛtānām api saṃskārāṇāṃ pratibandhī bhavati /
kasmāt, nirodhajaḥ saṃskāraḥ samādhijān saṃskārān bādhata iti /
nirodhasthitikālakramānubhavena nirodhacittakṛtasaṃskārāstitvam anumeyam /
vyutthānanirodhasamādhiprabhavaiḥ saha kaivalyabhāgīyaiḥ saṃskāraiś cittaṃ svasyāṃ prakṛtāv avasthitāyāṃ pravilīyate /

paraphrase: This [stilling] not only opposes samādhi-insight but obstructs even the impressions made by insight, because the impression born of stilling (nirodha) obstructs the impressions born of samādhi. The existence of impressions made by the stilled mind is to be inferred from experience of the sequence of the time of remaining in stilling. The mind, with the impressions of emergence, stilling and samādhi and along with those that conduce to kaivalya (kaivalya-bhāgīya), dissolves (pravilīyate) into its own source (prakṛti) as that stands. Those impressions, opposing the mind's office, are not causes of its staying. Since the mind, its office finished, turns back along with the kaivalya-conducing impressions, on that turning back the puruṣa, established in his own form alone, is called pure (śuddha), alone (kevala), free (mukta).
speaker: Vyāsa

indriyapraṇālikayā cittasya bāhyavastūparāgāt tadviṣayā sāmānyaviśeṣātmano 'rthasya viśeṣāvadhāraṇapradhānā vṛttiḥ pratyakṣaṃ pramāṇam /
phalam aviśiṣṭaḥ pauruṣeyaś cittavṛttibodhaḥ /
pratisaṃvedī puruṣa ity upariṣṭād upapādayiṣyāmaḥ /
anumeyasya tulyajātīyeṣv anuvṛtto bhinnajātīyebhyo vyāvṛttaḥ saṃbandho yas tadviṣayā sāmānyāvadhāraṇapradhānā vṛttir anumānam /
yathā deśāntaraprāpter gatimac candratārakaṃ caitravat, vindhyaś cāprāptir agatiḥ /
āptena dṛṣṭo 'numito vārthaḥ paratra svabodhasaṃkrāntaye śabdenopadiśyate, śabdāt tadarthaviṣayā vṛttiḥ śrotur āgamaḥ /
yasyāśraddheyārtho vaktā na dṛṣṭānumitārthaḥ sa āgamaḥ plavate /

original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: Perception is the mind's activity in which, coloured by an external thing through the channel of the senses, it takes as object a thing that is both general and particular, chiefly ascertaining the particular. Its fruit is the puruṣa's undifferentiated awareness of the mind's activity; the puruṣa is the witness of cognitions (pratisaṃvedin), to be established later. Inference is the activity that chiefly ascertains the general: its object is the relation of the inferable that runs through things of the same class and is absent from those of a different class. Example: the moon and stars move, because they reach other places, like Caitra; the Vindhya mountain does not reach other places and does not move. Testimony (āgama): a thing seen or inferred by a trustworthy person (āpta) is communicated by words so as to pass into another's understanding; the hearer's activity that has that thing as its object, arising from the words, is āgama. A testimony floats (plavate, is unreliable) when the speaker's meaning is not to be trusted and he has neither seen nor inferred it; with an original speaker who has seen or inferred the thing, it would not float.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

sa kasmān na pramāṇam /
yataḥ pramāṇena bādhyate /
bhūtārthaviṣayatvāt pramāṇasya /
tatra pramāṇena bādhanam apramāṇasya dṛṣṭam /
tadyathā dvicandradarśanaṃ sadviṣayeṇaikacandradarśanena bādhyata iti /
seyaṃ pañcaparvā bhavaty avidyā /
avidyāsmitārāgadveṣābhiniveśāḥ kleśā iti /

original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)

paraphrase: Why is error not valid cognition (pramāṇa)? Because it is sublated (bādhyate) by valid cognition, valid cognition having a real object. Here the sublation of the invalid by the valid is seen: for instance, seeing two moons is sublated by the seeing of one moon, which has a real object. This error has five joints (pañcaparvā): it is avidyā. Ignorance (avidyā), I-am-ness (asmitā), attachment (rāga), aversion (dveṣa) and clinging to life (abhiniveśa) are the afflictions (kleśa). These same, by their own names, are darkness (tamas), delusion (moha), great delusion (mahāmoha), gloom (tāmisra) and blind gloom (andhatāmisra). They will be set out on the occasion of the taints of the mind (citta-mala).
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

sa na pramāṇopārohī /
na viparyayopārohī ca /
vastuśūnyatve 'pi śabdajñānamāhātmyanibandhano vyavahāro dṛśyate /
tad yathā caitanyaṃ puruṣasya svarūpam iti /

bhavati ca vyapadeśe vṛttiḥ /
yathā caitrasya gaur iti /
tathā pratiṣiddhavastudharmo niṣkriyaḥ puruṣaḥ, tiṣṭhati bāṇaḥ sthāsyati sthita iti /

original.edition: GRETIL e-text 'pataJjali-yogasUtra-with-bhASya' (data entry Philipp A. Maas; based on K. Ś. Āgāśe's Ānandāśrama edition, 1904)
original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: It does not rise to valid cognition and does not rise to error. Though empty of a real thing, ordinary usage (vyavahāra) resting on the power of verbal knowledge is seen. Example: 'consciousness (caitanya) is the puruṣa's own nature'. When the puruṣa is consciousness (cit) itself, what is being said of what, and by what? Yet an activity occurs in the statement, as in 'Caitra's cow'. Likewise, in 'the puruṣa, having had the property of a thing denied, is without action': 'the arrow stands', 'will stand', 'stood' — when movement ceases, only the meaning of the verbal root is understood. And in 'the puruṣa is of the nature of non-origination', what is understood is only the absence of origination, not a property that belongs to the puruṣa. So that property is a construction (vikalpita), and ordinary usage exists through it.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: Yoga does not succeed for one without austerity (atapasvin). The impurity (aśuddhi), variegated by beginningless karma, afflictions and latent tendencies (vāsanā), and with a net of objects standing ready, cannot be broken up without austerity; hence austerity is taken up. And that austerity, it is held, should be practised by him in a way that does not harm the clarity of the mind (citta-prasādana). Self-study (svādhyāya) is the repetition (japa) of the purifying [syllables] beginning with the praṇava, or the study of the scriptures of liberation (mokṣa-śāstra). Devotion to Īśvara (īśvara-praṇidhāna) is the offering of all actions to the supreme teacher (parama-guru), or the renouncing of their fruit.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: The store of meritorious and demeritorious karma arises from desire (kāma), greed (lobha), delusion (moha) and anger (krodha). It is to be experienced either in the seen birth (dṛṣṭa-janma-vedanīya) or in the unseen birth. A meritorious store made with intense ardor by mantra, austerity and samādhi, or achieved by propitiating Īśvara, deities, great seers or those of great power, ripens at once. Likewise a demeritorious store, done repeatedly out of intense affliction against the frightened, the ill, the wretched, those who trust one, or those of great power and the ascetic, ripens at once. Examples: the boy Nandīśvara left his human form and was changed into divinity; likewise Nahuṣa, lord of the gods, left his own form and was changed into an animal. For those in hells there is no karma-store to be experienced in a seen birth; and for those whose afflictions are worn away there is none to be experienced in an unseen birth.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: While the afflictions exist, the store of karma begins to ripen; not when the root of affliction is cut. As rice grains still bound in their husk, whose seed-state is not burnt, are able to sprout, but not when the husk is removed or the seed burnt, so a karma-store bound by afflictions sprouts into ripening, not when the afflictions are removed or their seeds burnt by discerning insight. The ripening is threefold: birth (jāti), life-span (āyus) and experience (bhoga). The bhāṣya asks whether one karma causes one birth or many, and whether many karmas cause one birth or many, and rejects the alternatives: if each karma made one birth, the order of fruits of the beginningless, uncountable stored karma and of present karma would be unsettled and beings would have no assurance; if one karma caused many births, no time would remain for the rest; many karmas cannot cause many births at once, and if in sequence the earlier faults return. Therefore the varied store of merit and demerit made between one death and the next, standing as principal or secondary, becomes manifest at death, and, gathered by a single push (eka-praghaṭṭaka), completes death and produces just one birth; that birth gets its life-span from the same karma, and in that life-span experience arises from the same karma. Because it is the cause of birth, life-span and experience, that store is called 'of threefold ripening' (trivipāka). The bhāṣya goes on: this store is therefore called 'of one life' (ekabhavika). One to be experienced in the seen birth starts a single ripening, as cause of experience, or a double one, as cause of life-span and experience, as with Nandīśvara or Nahuṣa. The mind, by contrast, has been variegated since beginningless time by latent tendencies (vāsanā) produced by the experience of afflictions, karma and ripening, spread out on all sides like a fishing net with its knots; these vāsanās go back over many lives, whereas the karma-store is of one life, and the impressions that cause memory are the vāsanās, which are beginningless. The one-life store is of fixed (niyata) or unfixed (aniyata) ripening, and the rule stated holds only for what is to be experienced in the seen birth with fixed ripening. Unfixed karma to be experienced in an unseen birth has three courses: what was done but has not ripened is destroyed (as the black is destroyed here by the arising of the white); or it merges (āvāpa-gamana) into a principal karma; or it remains long, overpowered by a principal karma of fixed ripening. Because the place, time and cause of its ripening cannot be ascertained, the course of karma is varied and hard to know; yet an exception does not cancel the general rule, so the one-life karma-store is accepted.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: Every experience of pleasure is shot through with attachment (rāga) and depends on means, sentient or insentient (cetana-acetana); so there is a karma-store born of attachment. Likewise one hates the means of pain and is deluded, so there is a store born of aversion and delusion; and it is said that 'enjoyment does not arise without harming beings', so there is a bodily store made by harm (hiṃsā). Pleasure from objects is (as said) ignorance. Pleasure is the calm of the senses from satisfaction (tṛpti) in enjoyments; the failure to be calmed, from fickleness (laulya), is pain. The senses cannot be made free of thirst by the habit of enjoyment, because with the habit of enjoying, attachments and the skill of the senses grow; so the habit of enjoyment is not a means to pleasure. One who seeks pleasure, steeped in objects, is like one frightened of a scorpion's venom who is bitten by a snake: he sinks in a great mire of pain. This is called suffering of transformation (pariṇāma-duḥkhatā): being contrary (pratikūla) it torments only the yogin, even in the state of pleasure. Suffering of torment (tāpa-duḥkhatā): every experience of pain is shot through with aversion and depends on means; seeking the means of pleasure, one acts with body, speech and mind, and then favours or injures others, and by favour and injury heaps up dharma and adharma; that store arises from greed and delusion. Suffering of impression (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā): from the experience of pleasure there is a store of pleasure-impressions, and from the experience of pain a store of pain-impressions; so when the ripening of karma is experienced as pleasure or pain, a further store of karma is heaped up. Thus this beginningless stream of suffering, spread out, disturbs only the yogin, because it is by nature adverse (pratikūla); for the discerning person is like the eyeball (akṣi-pātra): a strand of wool laid on the eye pains by its touch but not on other limbs, so these sufferings afflict only the yogin, not the other person. The other takes up suffering brought by his own karma, drops what he has taken up and takes up again what he has dropped, as if pervaded by ignorance through a mind varied by beginningless tendencies; following the I-making and mine-making, he is followed in each birth by the threefold heats (tāpa) from external and inner causes. Seeing himself and the whole mass of beings being carried along by the beginningless stream of suffering, the yogin takes refuge in right seeing (samyag-darśana), the cause of the end of all suffering.

paraphrase: Also for the discerning everything is suffering because of the conflict of the functions of the guṇas. The guṇas of the buddhi, of the nature of illumination (prakhyā), activity (pravṛtti) and inertia (sthiti), cooperate with one another and produce a cognition (pratyaya) that is calm (śānta), terrible (ghora) or deluded (mūḍha), but always threefold. The functioning of the guṇas is unsteady (cala), so the mind is said to change quickly. The stronger forms and stronger functions conflict with one another, while the general ones proceed along with the stronger. So the guṇas, by mutual support, produce cognitions of pleasure, pain and delusion, all being of all forms; the difference among them is made by which guṇa is principal. Therefore, for the discerning, everything is suffering.

pradhānapuruṣayoḥ saṃyogo heyahetuḥ /
saṃyogasyātyantikī nivṛttir hānam /
hānopāyaḥ samyagdarśanam /
tatra hātuḥ svarūpam upādeyaṃ vā heyaṃ vā na bhavitum arhatīti hāne tasyocchedavādaprasaṅga upādāne ca hetuvādaḥ /

paraphrase: Ignorance (avidyā) is the seed of origin of this great mass of suffering; right seeing (samyag-darśana) is the cause of its absence. As the science of healing is fourfold — disease, cause of disease, health, medicine — so this śāstra is fourfold: saṃsāra, cause of saṃsāra, liberation (mokṣa), means of liberation. Of these, saṃsāra, full of suffering, is what is to be abandoned (heya); the conjunction (saṃyoga) of pradhāna and puruṣa is the cause of what is to be abandoned; the absolute ceasing of the conjunction is the abandonment (hāna); the means of abandonment is right seeing. Here the nature of the abandoner (hātṛ) can be neither to-be-taken nor to-be-abandoned: in abandoning it there would follow the doctrine of annihilation (uccheda-vāda); in taking it, the doctrine of causation (hetu-vāda); in rejecting both, the doctrine of eternity (śāśvata-vāda). This is right seeing.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: Past suffering, passed through by enjoyment, does not fall on the side of what is to be abandoned. Present suffering, mounted on enjoyment in its own moment, does not become something to be abandoned in another moment. So only the suffering not yet come afflicts the yogin who is like the eyeball, not the other knower; and that alone is to be abandoned.

dṛśyā buddhisattvopārūḍhāḥ sarve dharmāḥ /

anyasvarūpeṇa pratilabdhātmakaṃ svatantram api parārthatvāt paratantram /
tayor dṛgdarśanaśaktyor anādir arthakṛtaḥ saṃyogo heyahetur duḥkhasya kāraṇam ity arthaḥ /
tathā coktam --- tatsaṃyogahetuvivarjanāt syād ayam ātyantiko duḥkhapratīkāraḥ /
kasmāt, duḥkhahetoḥ parihāryasya pratīkāradarśanāt /
tadyathā --- pādatalasya bhedyatā, kaṇṭakasya bhettṛtvaṃ, parihāraḥ kaṇṭakasya pā(pa)dānadhiṣṭhānaṃ pādatrāṇavyavahitena vādhiṣṭhānam, etat trayaṃ yo veda loke sa tatra pratīkāram ārabhamāṇo bhedajaṃ duḥkhaṃ nāpnoti /
kasmāt, tritvopalabdhisāmarthyād iti /
atrāpi tāpakasya rajasaḥ sattvam eva tapyam /
kasmāt, tapikriyāyāḥ karmasthatvāt, sattve karmaṇi tapikriyā nāpariṇāmini niṣkriye kṣetrajñe, darśitaviṣayatvāt /

paraphrase: The seer is the puruṣa, the witness (pratisaṃvedin) of the buddhi. The seen is all properties (dharma) resting on buddhi-sattva. This seen, like a magnet-jewel (ayaskānta-maṇi), helps by mere nearness; by being seen it becomes the possession of the puruṣa, whose form is seeing, its master, since it has become an object of experience. Though it obtains its own being through another's form and is independent, it is dependent because it is for another. The beginningless, purpose-made conjunction of those two powers, the power of seeing and the power of sight, is the cause of what is to be abandoned, that is, of suffering. And it is said: 'By avoiding the cause of that conjunction there would be an absolute counteraction of suffering.' Why? Because for a suffering-cause that can be avoided a counteraction is seen: the sole of the foot can be pierced, a thorn can pierce, and the avoidance is not standing on the thorn, or standing on it with a shoe between. One who knows these three in the world, beginning the counteraction, does not get the pain born of piercing, since he can perceive the three. Here too, of rajas the heater, only sattva is heated (tapya), because the action of heating is in the object (karmastha). The heating is in sattva as object, not in the unchanging, inactive field-knower (kṣetrajña), since objects have been shown to him; but when sattva is heated, the puruṣa, following its form, is also heated afterwards.
speaker: Vyāsa

kriyāśīlaṃ rajaḥ sthitiśīlaṃ tama iti /
ete guṇāḥ parasparoparaktapravibhāgāḥ pariṇāminaḥ saṃyogaviyogadharmāṇa itaretaropāśrayeṇopārjitamūrtayaḥ parasparāṅgāṅgitve 'py asaṃbhinnaśaktipravibhāgās tulyajātīyātulyajātīyaśaktibhedānupātinaḥ pradhānavelāyām upadarśitasaṃnidhānā guṇatve 'pi ca vyāpāramātreṇa pradhānāntarṇītānumitāstitāḥ puruṣārthakartavyatayā prayuktasāmarthyāḥ saṃnidhimātropakāriṇo 'yaskāntamaṇikalpāḥ pratyayam antareṇaikatamasya vṛttim anuvartamānāḥ pradhānaśabdavācyā bhavanti /

tad etad bhūtendriyātmakaṃ bhūtabhāvena pṛthivyādinā sūkṣmasthūlena pariṇamate /
tathendriyabhāvena śrotrādinā sūkṣmasthūlena pariṇamata iti /
tat tu nāprayojanam api tu prayojanam urarīkṛtya pravartata iti bhogāpavargārthaṃ hi tad dṛśyaṃ puruṣasyeti /
tatreṣṭāniṣṭaguṇasvarūpāvadhāraṇam avibhāgāpannaṃ bhogo bhoktuḥ svarūpāvadhāraṇam apavarga iti /
dvayor atiriktam anyad darśanaṃ nāsti /
tathā coktam --- ayaṃ tu khalu triṣu guṇeṣu kartṛṣv akartari ca puruṣe tulyātulyajātīye caturthe tatkriyāsākṣiṇy upanīyamānān sarvabhāvān upapannān anupaśyann adarśanam anyac chaṅkata iti /
tāv etau bhogāpavargau buddhikṛtau buddhāv eva vartamānau kathaṃ puruṣe vyapadiśyete iti /
yathā vijayaḥ parājayo vā yoddhṛṣu vartamānaḥ svāmini vyapadiśyate, sa hi tatphalasya bhokteti

paraphrase: Sattva has the character of illumination; rajas, of activity; tamas, of inertia. These guṇas are coloured by one another in their divisions, transform, have the nature of conjunction and disjunction, take shape by mutual support, and, though each is a limb of the others, have powers that do not blend; they follow the division of like and unlike powers. When [one of them is] predominant (pradhāna-velā) their presence is shown; even when subordinate (guṇatve), their existence is inferred from their mere functioning as included in the predominant one; they are employed for the puruṣa's purpose, help by mere nearness like magnets, and following the working of any one without reliance on cognition are called by the name pradhāna. This is 'the seen'. It transforms as elements (bhūta) — earth and so on, subtle and gross — and as sense-faculties (indriya) — ear and so on, subtle and gross. It does not act without purpose but with a purpose accepted: for the seen exists for the puruṣa's enjoyment and liberation. Enjoyment (bhoga) is the ascertaining of the natures of desired and undesired qualities without distinction [from the seer]; liberation (apavarga) is the ascertaining of the nature of the enjoyer. There is no other seeing besides these two. It is said: 'This one, seeing all states brought before the three guṇas, which act, and the fourth, the non-acting puruṣa, like and unlike them and witness of their action, as fitting, suspects some other non-seeing.' How are enjoyment and liberation, made by the buddhi and abiding in the buddhi, attributed to the puruṣa? As victory or defeat abiding in the warriors is attributed to their master, who is the enjoyer of the fruit, so bondage and liberation, abiding in the buddhi, are attributed to the puruṣa. The buddhi's non-completion of the puruṣa's purpose is bondage; its ascertaining that purpose is liberation. By this, grasping, holding, reasoning-out, rejecting, knowledge of the real, and clinging (abhiniveśa) abiding in the buddhi are superimposed as existing in the puruṣa.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: The particularized (viśeṣa) are the elements (ākāśa, air, fire, water, earth), the five cognitive faculties (ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose), the five action faculties (speech, hand, foot, excretory organ, generative organ) and mind (manas) as the eleventh, serving every purpose: the sixteenfold particularized transformation of the guṇas. The six unparticularized (aviśeṣa) are the five tanmātras (sound, touch, form, taste, smell) and I-am-ness alone (asmitā-mātra). The mere mark (liṅga-mātra) is the great principle (mahat-tattva), being-alone (sattā-mātra), of which the six are transformations; the unmarked (aliṅga) is the unmanifest primal (pradhāna), 'neither being nor non-being', into which things dissolve on reabsorption. In the unmarked state, the purpose of the puruṣa is not a cause; in the three other stages it is, so they are called non-eternal. The guṇas follow all properties; they do not set or arise; they seem to arise and perish through their manifestations that come and go, like Devadatta 'becoming poor' when his cows die, from the death of the cows and not from any loss of himself. Each stage is mixed with the next nearer to the unmarked and is separated out from it in order; there is no further principle beyond the particularized, so the particularized undergo no further tattva-transformation; their transformations of property, mark and state will be explained later.

paraphrase: 'Seeing alone' means the power of the seer (dṛk-śakti) itself, untouched by any qualifier. That puruṣa is the witness (pratisaṃvedin) of the buddhi; he is neither of the same form as the buddhi nor utterly different. Not the same: the buddhi changes, since its objects are known or unknown; the puruṣa always has a known object, which shows that he is unchanging. The buddhi is for another (acts by combination); the puruṣa is for himself. The buddhi, since it determines every object, is threefold in guṇa and so non-conscious; the puruṣa is the overseer (upadraṣṭṛ) of the guṇas. Not utterly different: though pure, he looks on the cognitions (pratyaya) of the buddhi; looking at them, though not of their nature, he appears as if of their nature. It is said: 'The power of the enjoyer is unchanging and non-transferring (apratisaṃkramā); in the changing object it acts as if transferred and follows its activity; of that activity of the buddhi which has taken on the light of consciousness, by mere likeness the activity of knowing is called undistinguished from the buddhi's activity.'
speaker: Vyāsa

athāvidyā svacittena saha niruddhā svacittasyotpattibījam /

yatredam uktaṃ pradhānaṃ sthityaiva vartamānaṃ vikārākaraṇād apradhānaṃ syāt /
tathā gatyaiva vartamānaṃ vikāranityatvād apradhānaṃ syāt /
ubhayathā cāsya vṛttiḥ pradhānavyavahāraṃ labhate nānyathā /
kāraṇāntareṣv api kalpiteṣv eva samānaś carcaḥ /

ubhayasyāpy adarśanaṃ dharma ity eke /
tatredaṃ dṛśyasya svātmabhūtam api puruṣapratyayāpekṣaṃ darśanaṃ dṛśyadharmatvena bhavati /
tathā puruṣasyānātmabhūtam api dṛśyapratyayāpekṣaṃ puruṣadharmatvenevādarśanam avabhāsate /

original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: The puruṣa, the master, is conjoined with his own seen for the sake of seeing. The apprehension of the seen from that conjunction is enjoyment (bhoga); the apprehension of the seer's own form is liberation (apavarga). The conjunction ends when the work of seeing ends; so seeing is said to be the cause of disjunction; and seeing is the opposite of non-seeing (adarśana), so non-seeing is said to be the occasion of the conjunction. Here seeing is not the cause of liberation as something produced: by the mere absence of non-seeing there is absence of bondage, and that is liberation. When seeing arises, non-seeing, the cause of bondage, is destroyed; so seeing, that is knowledge, is called the cause of kaivalya. The bhāṣya then asks what this non-seeing is, and sets out views found in the śāstra: whether it is the guṇas' office (adhikāra); or the non-arising of the principal mind (pradhāna-citta) of the master whose form is seeing and to whom objects have been shown, that is, the absence of seeing while his own seen is present; or the purposiveness (arthavattā) of the guṇas; or ignorance stilled together with its own mind, the seed of the mind's arising; or the manifestation of the impression of movement when the impression of stillness is exhausted (on which a quotation says the pradhāna, if only still, would not be pradhāna, and if only moving, would not be pradhāna; its functioning gets the name of pradhāna in both ways). Some say seeing-power itself is non-seeing, on the authority of a scripture that the pradhāna's activity is for the sake of making the self known; some say non-seeing is a property of both; some say knowledge itself is non-seeing. These are the alternatives found in the śāstra; the plurality of alternatives concerns the conjunction of all puruṣas with the guṇas in general.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: 'Ignorance' means the latent tendency (vāsanā) of erroneous knowledge (viparyaya-jñāna). The buddhi, imbued with that tendency, does not reach the discernment of the puruṣa (puruṣa-khyāti), its completed work, and returns still holding its office. But when it does reach that discernment, its office finished and non-seeing ceased, it does not return, since the cause of bondage is absent. Someone [an opponent] makes the point with the tale of the impotent man: the foolish wife says, 'Impotent one, noble sir, my sister has children; why not I?' He replies, 'When I am dead I will beget a child on you.' So the knowledge that exists does not bring about the cessation of the mind; what hope that it will when it has been destroyed? One who is almost a teacher (ācāryadeśīya) replies: is not liberation just the cessation of the buddhi, since with the cause of non-seeing absent, the buddhi ceases? Non-seeing, the cause of bondage, is turned back by seeing. So the cessation of the mind is liberation; why this misplaced confusion of mind?

eṣā catuṣṭayī kāryā vimuktiḥ prajñāyāḥ /
cittavimuktis tu trayī caritādhikārā buddhiḥ /
guṇā giriśikharataṭacyutā iva grāvāṇo niravasthānāḥ svakāraṇe pralayābhimukhāḥ saha tenāstaṃ gacchanti /
na caiṣāṃ pravilīnānāṃ punar asty utpādaḥ prayojanābhāvād iti /
etasyām avasthāyāṃ guṇasaṃbandhātītaḥ svarūpamātrajyotir amalaḥ kevalī puruṣa iti /
etāṃ saptavidhāṃ prāntabhūmiprajñām anupaśyan puruṣaḥ kuśala ity ākhyāyate /
pratiprasave 'pi cittasya muktaḥ kuśala ity eva bhavati guṇātītatvād iti

paraphrase: 'For him' refers back to the one in whom discernment has risen. It is sevenfold when, impurity and covering being gone and no other cognition arising, the discerning person's insight has seven forms: (1) what is to be abandoned is fully known, nothing more to be known; (2) the causes of what is to be abandoned are worn away, nothing more to be worn away; (3) abandonment has been realised by the samādhi of stilling (nirodha-samādhi); (4) the means of abandonment, discernment, has been cultivated. This fourfold is the liberation of insight, accomplished (kāryā vimukti). The liberation of the mind (citta-vimukti) is threefold: (5) the buddhi's office is done; (6) the guṇas, like boulders fallen from a mountain peak, have no footing, turn toward dissolution into their cause, and go to their setting along with it; (7) once dissolved, there is no further arising of them, for lack of purpose. In this state the puruṣa is beyond connection with the guṇas, light of his own form only, stainless, alone (kevalin). The puruṣa who looks on this sevenfold insight of the final stage is called skilful (kuśala); even at the reabsorption of the mind he is liberated and skilful, being beyond the guṇas.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: The eight limbs of yoga (yogāṅga) are to be taught. By practising them, the impurity (aśuddhi), which is fivefold error (viparyaya), is destroyed; when it is destroyed, right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) becomes manifest. As the means are practised, so the impurity thins; as it wears away, the light of knowledge grows in order with the wearing away; that growth reaches its highest in the discerning awareness (viveka-khyāti), that is, up to the knowledge of the nature of the guṇas and the puruṣa. The practice of the limbs is the cause of separation from impurity, as an axe is of what is cut; and the cause of attaining discerning awareness, as dharma is of pleasure. The śāstra has nine kinds of cause, and a verse gives them: origin (utpatti), support (sthiti), manifestation (abhivyakti), modification (vikāra), cognition (pratyaya), attainment (āpti), separation (viyoga), otherness (anyatva), sustaining (dhṛti). Examples: the mind is the cause of origin for cognition; the puruṣa's purpose is the cause of the mind's support, as food is of the body; light is the cause of manifestation of form, and so is the cognition of form; another object is the cause of modification of the mind, as fire of the cooked; smoke-knowledge is cause of cognition of fire; the practice of the limbs is cause of attainment of discerning awareness, and also of separation from impurity; a goldsmith is cause of otherness for gold; and, in one cognition of a woman, ignorance is cause to deludedness, aversion to pain, attachment to pleasure, knowledge of truth to impartiality; the body is the sustaining cause of the faculties, and so on. Practice of the limbs of yoga is cause in only two ways: separation (from impurity) and attainment (of discernment).

paraphrase: Non-harming (ahiṃsā) is the absence of hostility (anabhidroha) toward all beings, in every way and at all times. The later restraints and observances have it as their root; they are taught for its sake, are taken up to make it pure. It is said: 'As this Brāhmaṇa takes up more and more vows, so, turning away from what is done through heedlessness and has harm as its source, he makes that same non-harming pure of form.' Truthfulness (satya) is speech and mind that are in accord with the fact (yathārtha): as seen, as inferred, so speech and mind. Speech is uttered to pass one's understanding to another; if it is not deceived, mistaken or barren of understanding, it is truthful; it is spoken for the benefit of all beings, not to injure them. If, even when so spoken, it were only a harm to beings, it would not be truth but sin, and one would reach grievous darkness through that mere semblance of merit. So one should speak, after examining, the truth that is for the good of all beings. Stealing (steya) is taking others' goods contrary to the scripture; its prohibition, in the form of absence of longing (aspṛhā), is non-stealing (asteya). Continence (brahmacarya) is restraint of the generative organ in one whose senses are guarded. Non-possessiveness (aparigraha) is non-acceptance of objects, on seeing the faults of acquiring, keeping, losing, attachment and harming in them. These are the restraints.

paraphrase: Non-harming limited by class (jāti) is a fisherman's harming fish only, not elsewhere. Limited by place (deśa): 'I will not kill in a holy place.' Limited by time (kāla): 'I will not kill on the fourteenth day or on a holy day.' Limited by occasion (samaya): one who has stopped harming in those three, saying 'I will kill only for a god or a Brāhmaṇa, not otherwise'; and as with warriors, harm in battle only and not elsewhere. Being unbroken in all grounds (bhūmi) and all objects, in every way, they are called universal (sārvabhauma), the great vow (mahāvrata).

paraphrase: External purity (śauca) is that produced by earth, water and the like, and the eating of what is clean; inner purity is washing away the taints of the mind (citta-mala). Contentment (saṃtoṣa) is not wishing to take more than the means at hand. Austerity (tapas) is bearing the pairs of opposites (dvandva): hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, silence of wood (kāṣṭha-mauna) and silence of gesture (ākāra-mauna); its vows, as fits, are the kṛcchra, cāndrāyaṇa and sāṃtapana and the like. Self-study (svādhyāya) is study of the scriptures of liberation or repetition of the praṇava. Devotion to Īśvara (īśvara-praṇidhāna) is offering all actions to that supreme teacher. A verse is quoted: 'Whether lying, sitting or going on the road, being at ease, his web of harmful thoughts (vitarka) worn away, seeing the wearing away of the seed of saṃsāra, let him be ever united and a sharer in the enjoyment of the immortal.' It is said of this: 'from that comes realization of the inward consciousness and the absence of obstacles' (1.29).
