paraphrase: Violence is threefold: done (kṛta), caused to be done (kārita), approved (anumodita). Each is again threefold, from greed (lobha, e.g. for meat or skin), from anger ('he wronged me'), or from delusion ('it will be dharma for me'); greed, anger and delusion are each mild, middling or intense. So violence has twenty-seven forms; the mild, middling and intense are again each threefold, making eighty-one; and with rules, options and combinations it is countless, since the kinds of living beings are countless. The same applies to untruth and the rest. 'Suffering and ignorance without end as fruit' is the cultivation of the opposite: the violent one first takes away the victim's strength, then torments him by the fall of a weapon, then deprives him of life. From robbing strength, his own animate and inanimate implements lose strength; from causing suffering he suffers in hells, animal births and ghost-states; and from robbing life, moment by moment at the end of his own life, wishing for death, he still breathes somehow, because the ripening of suffering is fixed. If somehow such violence goes with merit, then in gaining pleasure he will have a short life. The same is to be applied, as fits, to untruth and the rest. Thus contemplating the unwanted ripening that follows harmful thoughts, one should not set the mind on them.

tathā vicchidya vicchidya tena tenātmanā punaḥ punaḥ samudācarantīti vicchinnāḥ /

na hi rāgakāle krodhaḥ samudācarati /

kas tarhi vicchinnaḥ prasuptas tanur udāro vā kleśa iti, ucyate --- satyam evaitat, kiṃtu viśiṣṭānām evaiteṣāṃ vicchinnāditvam /
yathaiva pratipakṣabhāvanāto nivṛttas tathaiva svavyañjakāñjanenābhivyakta iti /
sarva evāmī kleśā avidyābhedāḥ /
kasmāt, sarveṣv avidyaivābhiplavate /
yad avidyayā vastv ākāryate tad evānuśerate kleśā viparyāsapratyayakāla upalabhyante kṣīyamāṇāṃ cāvidyām anu kṣīyanta iti

original.licence: GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (attribution); short excerpt only

paraphrase: Here ignorance is the field (kṣetra), the ground of origin, of the later ones — I-am-ness and the rest — which have four varieties: dormant, attenuated, interrupted, fully active. Dormancy (prasupti) is the afflictions' having reached a seed-state (bīja-bhāva), resting in the mind as bare potency (śakti-mātra); their awakening (prabodha) is their coming face to face with a support (ālambana). For one with discerning insight (prasaṃkhyāna) whose seeds of affliction are burnt, even when the support is present the affliction does not arise again; how could a burnt seed sprout? Hence one 'whose afflictions are worn away, skilful, in his last body (carama-deha)' is spoken of; in him alone is that fifth state of the afflictions, the burnt-seed state. Attenuation (tanutva): afflictions struck by the cultivation of their opposite (pratipakṣa-bhāvanā) become thin. Interrupted (vicchinna): they act again and again in this or that form, cut off; e.g. at a time of passion anger is not seen, though passion, seen in one place, is not absent in another — Caitra, enamoured of one woman, is not thereby disenchanted with the others; there passion has gained activity, elsewhere it will gain it; so at that time it is dormant, attenuated and interrupted. Fully active (udāra): the one that has gained activity in regard to an object. All these do not go beyond being of the sphere of the afflictions. The bhāṣya notes that these four belong to particular afflictions in particular circumstances: as one is turned back by the cultivation of the opposite, so it becomes manifest through its own manifester's coloration. All the afflictions are varieties of ignorance, because ignorance pervades in all: what ignorance makes appear as a thing, that the afflictions lie along with; they are found at the time of a cognition of error, and are worn away as ignorance is worn away.
speaker: Vyāsa

notes: The four states of the afflictions (dormant, attenuated, interrupted, fully active), with Vyāsa's fifth state, the burnt-seed (dagdha-bīja) state, found only in one of the last body (caramadeha). Vyāsa's descriptions of how each state shows itself are recorded in phenomenology (phn:ys-klesa-state-*): dormant = potency only, awakens on meeting a support; attenuated = thinned by cultivating the opposite; interrupted = passion and anger do not occur together, passion is held for one object while dormant for others; fully active = has gained activity toward an object. The middle of the passage (an objection and reply on the distinction of the states) is compressed.

paraphrase: When posture is mastered, inhalation is the drawing in of outer air and exhalation the expelling of inner air; the cutting off of their movement, the absence of both, is prāṇāyāma. It is external (absence of movement after exhalation), internal (after inhalation), or a third, stationary one, in which both cease at once through a single effort, as water on a hot stone contracts on all sides. Each is observed by place (its range), time (a measure of moments) and number (of breaths), as mild, middling or intense, and so practised becomes long and subtle. The fourth comes gradually through mastery of the stages, after the spheres of inhalation and exhalation have been ascertained and passed beyond.

paraphrase: Ignorance is the appearing of permanence in an impermanent effect: e.g. 'the earth is fixed; the sky with moon and stars is fixed; the dwellers in heaven are immortal.' Likewise the appearing of purity in the impure, the utterly disgusting body — 'the wise know the body to be impure because of its place, its seed, its support, its outflow, its end, and because its purity has to be supplied' [quoted verse]. The text illustrates this with a young woman who is perceived (jñāyate) as lovely, 'like a new crescent of the moon, as if made of honey and nectar', and asks what is connected with what (kasya kena abhisaṃbandhaḥ); so arises the inverted cognition (viparyāsa-pratyaya) of the pure in the impure. By this the cognition of merit in demerit and of the useful in the useless is also explained. Likewise the appearing of pleasure in pain; the sūtra will say later [YS 2.15]: 'everything is suffering for the discerning, because of the sufferings of transformation, torment and impression, and because of the conflict of the functions of the guṇas'. And the appearing of self in the not-self: in external instruments, sentient or insentient (cetana-acetana), in the body as the seat of enjoyment, in the puruṣa's instrument, the mind (manas). It is said here: 'One who takes sattva, manifest or unmanifest, to be self rejoices at its prosperity, thinking it his own prosperity, and grieves at its calamity, thinking it his own calamity; he is wholly unawakened (apratibuddha).' This fourfold ignorance is the root of the whole chain of afflictions and of the store of karma with its ripening. Its true nature is to be understood like 'non-friend' (amitra) and 'cow-track' (goṣpada): as a non-friend is neither the absence of a friend nor merely a friend but a rival opposed to him, and a cow-track is neither the absence of a cow's track nor the mere track but a place different from both, so ignorance is neither valid cognition nor the absence of valid cognition, but another cognition contrary to knowledge (vidyā).
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: The external (bāhya) is the absence of movement that follows exhalation; the internal (ābhyantara) is the absence of movement that follows inhalation; the third, the suspended operation (stambha-vṛtti), is where both are absent, brought about by a single effort — as water dropped on a hot stone shrinks on all sides, so movement of both stops at once. All three are said to be regulated (paridṛṣṭa) by place (deśa), time (kāla) and number (saṃkhyā); Vyāsa glosses each only in general terms (the extent of its field, a limit in moments, and a count of breaths in successive 'strokes' (udghāta), graded mild, middling and intense) and gives no figures. Practised so, it becomes long and subtle.

paraphrase: The external, fixed by place, time and number, is surpassed (ākṣipta); so too the internal, fixed by place, time and number, is surpassed; in both ways it is long and subtle. The third differs: its stopping is begun once, without attention to an object, regulated by place, time and number, long and subtle. The fourth is the stopping preceded by the surpassing of both, gradually, by mastery of ground, after determining the object of inhalation and exhalation; this is the difference.

paraphrase: The puruṣa is the power of the seer (dṛk-śakti); the buddhi is the power of seeing (darśana-śakti). The seeming coming-together of the two into a single form is called the affliction I-am-ness. When the powers of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, utterly distinct and utterly unmixed, are as if reached in non-separation, then enjoyment (bhoga) is possible. But when they attain their own forms, only kaivalya comes about; where would enjoyment be? The bhāṣya answers objections (that the bearer would be unchanging, that the paths would be mixed, that the condition-transformation would make things unchanging) and illustrates with clay becoming lump and pot. paraphrase: The bhāṣya first sets out the seven worlds and their beings at length: the earth-world from the Avīci hell up to the back of Meru, with the six great hells, the seven nether worlds and the seven-continent earth around Meru; the intermediate space of planets and stars; heaven (svar), the Mahendra world with six classes of gods; the great world (mahar) of Prajāpati; and the three Brahma-worlds (Jana, Tapas, Satya), whose gods live on meditation and, in the Satya world, are marked by savitarka, savicāra, ānanda-only and asmitā-only meditation-happiness. paraphrase: The bhāṣya lays out five forms of the elements. The first, the gross, is the particular things such as sound with shape and other properties. The second, own-form, is the common character: solidity of earth, fluidity of water, heat of fire, motion of air, all-pervasiveness of ākāśa. The third, the subtle, is the subtle element (tanmātra), the cause of the element, one part of which is the atom (paramāṇu). The fourth, pervasion, is the guṇas, whose nature is illumination, activity and stability, following the nature of their effects. The fifth, purposiveness, is the being-for-experience-and-release (bhoga-apavarga) that runs through the guṇas. From saṃyama on these five forms in the five elements, in turn, the seeing of each form's own nature and its mastery arise; having mastered the five forms of the elements, one becomes master of the elements; from that mastery the natures of the elements follow his intention (saṃkalpa) like cows following a calf.

teṣu pralīneṣu puruṣaḥ punar idaṃ tāpatrayaṃ na bhuṅkte /
tad eteṣāṃ guṇānāṃ manasi karmakleśavipākasvarūpeṇābhivyaktānāṃ caritārthānāṃ pratiprasave puruṣasyātyantiko guṇaviyogaḥ kaivalyaṃ tadā svarūpapratiṣṭhā citiśaktir eva puruṣa iti.

When they are dissolved, puruṣa no longer undergoes this threefold suffering (tāpa-traya). When the guṇas, which had manifested in the mind as karma, affliction and ripening, and have served their purpose, return to their source (pratiprasava), there is the absolute separation of puruṣa from the guṇas: kaivalya. Then puruṣa is the power of consciousness (citi-śakti) established in its own form.

paraphrase: The bhāṣya says there are four kinds of yogin: the prāthamakalpika, the madhubhūmika, the one whose insight is a light (prajñājyotis) and the one who has passed beyond what is to be cultivated (atikrānta-bhāvanīya). The first is the practiser whose light has just begun; the second is the one of truth-bearing insight (ṛtaṃbharā prajñā); the third is the master of elements and senses, who has made a protective binding over everything cultivated and to be cultivated; for the fourth the one aim is the return of the mind to its source (citta-pratisarga), and his is the sevenfold insight of the last stage. To a brāhmaṇa realising the madhumatī stage, gods of high stations (sthānin), seeing the purity of his sattva, extend invitations with their stations: 'sit here, enjoy here', this pleasure, this maiden, an elixir (rasāyana) that defeats old age and death, a sky-vehicle, wishing-trees, the sacred Mandākinī, siddhas and great seers, agreeable apsarases, divine ear and eye, a body like a diamond: 'all this you have earned by your own qualities; take up this imperishable, ageless, deathless station dear to the gods.'

paraphrase: Thus addressed, he should reflect on the faults of attachment: cooked in the terrible coals of saṃsāra and turning in the darkness of birth and death, he has somehow obtained the lamp of yoga that destroys the darkness of the afflictions, and these winds of sense-objects, born of craving, are its opponents; having obtained the light, how should he, deceived by this mirage of sense-objects, make himself fuel again for the blazing fire of saṃsāra? 'Farewell, sense-objects, like dreams, sought by wretched people.' With his mind thus settled he should cultivate samādhi. Having made no attachment, he should not even feel pride ('even the gods seek me'): through pride he would think himself well established and would not regard himself as seized by death by the hair. And heedlessness (pramāda), watching for a gap and to be guarded against with constant effort, having found an opening would stir up the afflictions, and then again there is the prospect of the undesirable. For one who makes neither attachment nor pride, the cultivated aim will be firm and the aim to be cultivated will come to face him.

paraphrase: There is no aggregation of things in the moment and its sequence; muhūrta, day and night and the like are aggregations made by the intellect (buddhi-samāhāra). This time, though empty of a real thing (vastu-śūnya), is a construction of the intellect, following word-cognition, and appears to ordinary people with outgoing vision as if it were the own-form of a thing. But the moment is real (vastu-patita) and bound up with sequence (kramāvalambin), and sequence is the immediacy of moments; this the yogins who know time call 'time'. Sequence is the immediacy of a moment after the earlier one; two moments do not exist together, so only the one present moment exists and no earlier or later moments, and hence there is no aggregate of moments. Past and future moments are to be explained as accompanied by transformation; by that one moment the whole world undergoes transformation, and all these properties rest on that moment. From saṃyama on the moment and its sequence comes direct realisation of them, and from that knowledge born of discrimination arises.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: Knowledge of the truth should be free of doubt; therefore the sūtra says that the discernment is from knowledge born of discrimination. The bhāṣya illustrates with a cow and a mare (difference of class), two cows alike in class and place (difference of characteristic) and two myrobalan fruits alike in class and characteristic (difference of place); it adds that when, while the knower's attention is elsewhere (anya-vyagra), the first fruit is moved into the second's place, the place being the same, the distinction 'this is earlier, this later' cannot be made. How then? The place together with the moment of the earlier fruit differs from the place together with the moment of the later, and the two fruits differ by their experience of their own place-and-moment. By this example, when an atom alike in class, characteristic and place takes the place of an earlier atom, the masterful yogin (īśvara yogin), having directly perceived the earlier atom's place together with its moment, has the cognition of their otherness from the difference of the co-present moment.
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: Tāraka means arisen from one's own prātibha, not taught by instruction (anaupadeśika). 'All objects' means that nothing is outside its range. 'In every way' means that it knows everything, past, future and present, through all their modifications. 'Without sequence' means that it grasps everything in every way in one moment. This discrimination-born knowledge is complete; the lamp of yoga, from the madhumatī stage up to its completion, is a part of it.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: When the intellect-sattva, with the stain of rajas and tamas shaken off, has as its only remaining scope the cognition of the distinctness of puruṣa and its seeds of affliction are burnt, it comes as if to a likeness of purity with puruṣa; the purity of puruṣa is the absence of figurative (upacarita) experience. In this state kaivalya occurs, whether for the one who has lordship (īśvara) or not, whether he has shared in discrimination-born knowledge or not; for one whose seeds of affliction are burnt no further need of knowledge remains. The power and knowledge born of samādhi were begun by way of the purity of sattva. In ultimate truth it is by knowledge that non-seeing (adarśana) is removed; with that removed, no further afflictions; with no afflictions, no ripening of karma; and in this state the guṇas, their office finished, no longer present themselves to puruṣa as something seen. That is puruṣa's kaivalya: then puruṣa is a light of its own form alone, stainless, isolated (kevalī).
speaker: Vyāsa
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted

paraphrase: Saṃyama is applied to the stage that comes immediately next after the stage mastered. One who has not mastered the lower stage and, skipping the next, tries saṃyama on the far stages does not obtain it, and then how could he have the light of insight? Of one who through the grace of Īśvara (īśvara-prasāda) has already mastered a higher stage, saṃyama on lower stages, such as knowledge of another's mind, is not fitting, since that purpose is known in another way. That this stage is next to that one, in this yoga itself is the teacher (upādhyāya); as it is said: 'By yoga yoga is to be known; yoga advances out of yoga; he who is unheedful (apramatta) through yoga delights long in yoga.'
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: The impressions of emergence are properties of the mind, not of the nature of cognition (pratyaya); so when cognitions are restrained they are not restrained; the impressions of restraint are also properties of the mind. Between these two there is suppression and emergence: the impressions of emergence dwindle, the impressions of restraint are laid down. The mind follows into the moment of restraint; this changing (anyathātva) of the impressions in one mind moment by moment is the transformation of restraint. The mind then has only impressions left (saṃskāra-śeṣa), as explained in [the account of] restraint-samādhi.

paraphrase: Others hold that the mind, like a lamp in a jar or a palace, contracts and expands and is only of the size of the body, so that an intermediate state (antarābhāva) and saṃsāra are logical. The teacher (ācārya) says that it is the function (vṛtti) of the all-pervading (vibhu) mind that contracts and expands, and this depends on dharma and the like as occasion. Occasion is twofold, external and internal: external depends on means such as the body (praise, gift, salutation), internal depends on the mind alone (faith and the like). As was said, the 'abodes' of meditators (friendliness and the rest) bring about exalted dharma without help from external means; of the two the mental is stronger: what surpasses knowledge and dispassion, and who else could empty the Daṇḍaka forest by bodily action without the strength of mind, or drink the ocean like Agastya?
speaker: Vyāsa

na hy avasitādhikāre manasi nirāśrayā vāsanāḥ sthātum utsahante /
yad abhimukhībhūtaṃ vastu yāṃ vāsanāṃ vyanakti tasyās tadālambanam /

paraphrase: The cause (hetu): from dharma, pleasure; from adharma, pain; from pleasure, attachment; from pain, aversion; from these, effort, by which, moving by mind, speech or body, one favours or harms another; from that again dharma and adharma, pleasure and pain, attachment and aversion. Thus this six-spoked wheel of saṃsāra turns; ignorance (avidyā) is its leader and the root of all the afflictions. The fruit is that on which the presentness of dharma and the rest depends. The support (āśraya) is the mind with its office still to be done: when the mind's office is finished, the vāsanās, having no support, cannot remain. The object (ālambana) is whatever thing coming to the fore manifests a vāsanā. All vāsanās are held together by these four, and when they are absent the vāsanās depending on them are absent.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: The future is that whose manifestation is to come; the past that whose manifestation has been experienced; the present that which has risen to its own function; these three are objects of knowledge. If they did not exist in their own form, this cognition would arise without an object; therefore the past and future exist in their own form. Also, if the fruit of karma about to arise were unreal (nirupākhya), skilful action aimed at it would not be fitting. The cause is able to make an existing fruit present, not to produce it anew; it only gives a special favour to what depends on it. The bearer (dharmin) has many properties, established in the different paths. The past and future are not present in the manner of the present, with a special manifestation; they exist by the own-form that is to be manifested, or by the own-form of manifestation once experienced. The own-form-manifestation belongs to the present path only. At any time two paths are always attended by the bearer, so the three paths do not come into being from non-existence.
speaker: Vyāsa

prakhyākriyāsthitiśīlānāṃ guṇānāṃ grahaṇātmakānāṃ karaṇabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śrotram indriyaṃ, grāhyātmakānāṃ śabdatanmātrabhāvenaikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ śabdo viṣaya iti, śabdādīnāṃ mūrtisamānajātīyānām ekaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivīparamāṇus tanmātrāvayavas teṣāṃ caikaḥ pariṇāmaḥ pṛthivī gaur vṛkṣaḥ parvata ityevamādir bhūtāntareṣv api snehauṣṇyapraṇāmitvāvakāśadānāny upādāya sāmānyam ekavikārārambhaḥ samādheyaḥ /

paraphrase: The guṇas of illumination, activity and stability have one transformation as the instrument in the form of the sense of hearing, and one transformation as the object in the form of sound (śabda-tanmātra); likewise for earth atoms and the rest, the one transformation of like-natured things ends in earth, cow, tree, mountain. The bhāṣya then reports the argument 'there is no object unaccompanied by cognition, but there is cognition unaccompanied by an object, imagined in dream and the like'; those who by this line deny the own-nature of a thing, saying it is a mere conceptual construction like a dream object and does not exist in ultimate truth, are asked how, giving up the thing's own form by the force of conceptual cognition that is not a means of knowledge (apramāṇa), and denying that very thing which stands present in its own greatness, they could be worthy of belief.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: One common object is the support of many minds; it is not imagined by one mind nor by many minds but stands on itself (sva-pratiṣṭha). How: with the object the same, the cognition differs by the mind: one relying on dharma has cognition of pleasure, one relying on adharma has cognition of pain, one relying on ignorance has deluded cognition, one relying on right seeing has cognition of indifference. An object imagined by one mind cannot colour another's mind. So the path of the object and the path of the cognition, distinguished as grasped and grasping, are separate, with no trace of mixing. On the Sāṃkhya side the object is of three guṇas and moving, connected with minds according to dharma and the like as occasion, and is the cause of the cognition that arises in the form fitting that occasion. Some say the object arises together with cognition because it is enjoyable like pleasure; by this line, obstructing commonness, they deny the form of the object in the earlier and later moments.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: If the object depended on one mind, then when that mind was distracted or restrained, the object's own form, untouched by it, not the object of another, without evidence and not grasped by anyone, would then be what? And when connected again with the mind, whence would it arise? Its parts not then present would not exist, so there would be no back and even the belly would not be grasped. Therefore the object is independent, common to all puruṣas, and minds are independent, working separately in each puruṣa; from the connection of the two comes apprehension, which is the experience (bhoga) of puruṣa.

paraphrase: As the other senses and their objects, being seen, are not self-luminous, so the mind is to be understood. Fire is no example: fire does not illuminate a form of its own that was unlit; light is seen in the conjunction of what is illuminated and what illuminates, and there is no conjunction in mere own-form. If the mind were self-luminous it would be ungraspable by anyone, as ākāśa is established in itself and not in another. But the activity of beings is seen from the awareness of the course of their own intellect ('I am angry, I am afraid, here is my attachment, there my anger'), which would not be fitting if one's own intellect were not grasped.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: If a mind were grasped by another mind, by what would the cognition of cognition (buddhi-buddhi) be grasped, and that by another, and that by another: a regress. And memory would be confused: as many memories as there are experiences of these cognitions, and from the confusion there would be no ascertainment of one memory. Thus by the annihilationists (vaināśika), who deny the puruṣa who is aware of the intellect, everything is thrown into confusion; they, imagining an experiencer anywhere, do not cohere by reason. Some, imagining even a 'being' (sattva) who lays down these five aggregates and takes up others, still fear it; and having said 'I shall live the celibate life at the teacher's feet for great disgust with the aggregates, dispassion, non-arising and tranquillity', they then deny the being. The Sāṃkhya-Yoga and other doctrines, by their own word, accept puruṣa as the lord of the mind and the experiencer.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: The mind is coloured by the object to be thought, and, itself being an object, is connected by its own function with puruṣa the subject. This one mind, coloured by seer and seen, shining as both object and subject, having taken on the form of the sentient and the insentient (cetana-acetana), object-natured yet as if not, insentient yet as if sentient, like a crystal jewel, is called 'all-objective'. Deluded by this likeness of the mind, some say the mind itself is the sentient one; others say all this is mind only and there is no world of cows and pots with causes; they are to be pitied, because they have as their seed of delusion the mind shining with the forms of all things. In the insight of samādhi the known object, reflected, is other than the mind, since it is its support; if that object were mind alone, how could the insight determine its own form by insight itself? Therefore the puruṣa by whom the reflected object in the insight is determined exists. Those who distinguish, by class, grasper, grasping and grasped as three differing forms of the mind are right-seers, and by them puruṣa is reached.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: This mind, though variegated by countless vāsanās, is for another, for that other's experience and release, not for itself, because it acts in combination, like a house. A mind that acts in combination cannot be for its own sake: the mind of pleasure is not for pleasure, knowledge is not for knowledge; both are for another. The puruṣa who is meaningful by experience and release is the other; not the other as mere generality. Whatever mere-generality 'other' an annihilationist might offer would itself, acting in combination, be only for another. But this special other is puruṣa, who does not act in combination.

Or, as the same farmer cannot make water and earth-juices enter the roots of the crop but only removes the weeds, so dharma is the cause only of the removal of adharma, since purity and impurity are utterly opposed, and is not the cause of the natures' activity. paraphrase: The immovable eternity is puruṣa's, the transforming eternity that of the guṇas: that in which, while it transforms, the reality (tattva) is not destroyed is eternal, and both are eternal because their reality is not struck. In the properties of the guṇas such as the intellect, sequence is grasped by the end of transformation and has a final limit; in the guṇas as eternal bearers it has no final limit. For liberated puruṣas, eternal and immovable, established in mere own-form, the being in own-form is experienced only as sequence, imagined by following the word for existence, and there too has no final limit. The bhāṣya then treats the question whether saṃsāra, abiding and moving in the guṇas, has an end of sequence. It sorts questions: 'will everyone born die?' is answered categorically ('yes'); 'will everyone who dies be born?' is answered by distinction (the skilled one whose discrimination-vision has arisen and whose thirst is exhausted will not be born, the other will); 'is human birth better?' is answered by distinction (better than animals, not better than gods and seers). The question 'is this saṃsāra finite or endless?' is called one not answerable as posed (avacanīya); for the skilled one there is an end of the sequence of saṃsāra, not for the other, and fixing on either alone is a fault. Therefore this question is to be answered by analysis (vyākaraṇīya).
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: The example given is the rise of the ripening of the kind called vṛṣadaṃśa, manifested by its own manifester (vyañjaka). Even if it is separated by a hundred births, by distance, or by a hundred aeons, it arises immediately when its manifester arises again, taking up the vāsanās shaped by the earlier experienced ripening.
speaker: Vyāsa

paraphrase: Invocation: may the god, the lord of serpents, protect you — he who, leaving his first form, appears in many ways to favour the world; whose mass of afflictions is destroyed; many-mouthed, the source of all knowledge, white and spotless in body, joined with yoga and the giver of yoga.
